title: Australian investor home lending plunges 32% in Q3 as tax curbs and RBA hikes bite harder
summary: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold. - Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing. body: A drop in home lending this sharp gives the RBA more evidence that its five hikes this year are biting. That supports the case for a pause after November’s split decision, and it is a modest headwind for the Australian dollar. Short-dated Australian government bond yields may be sensitive to any further sign that housing is cooling faster than the central bank expects. Bank stocks face slower mortgage growth, especially in investor lending, which has traditionally been a profitable segment. With energy-driven inflation still the RBA’s main worry, oil prices remain the swing factor for whether housing weakness is enough to keep rates on hold. Tax changes, lending caps and five rate hikes have all hit Australian property investors at once, and the result is a collapse in landlord borrowing. The value of new Australian home loans fell 15.5% in the September quarter, nearly twice the 8% decline economists had expected, as lending to property investors collapsed in the wake of government tax changes and a year of Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes. Investor lending was the main drag, plunging 32.3% on the quarter after a 10.2% fall in the June quarter. Owner-occupier loan values fell a more modest 5.3%, following a 1.9% decline previously. The overall drop was a sharp acceleration from the 5.2% fall recorded in the prior quarter. The split between investors and owner-occupiers suggests policy is doing much of the work. In the May federal budget, the government moved to end negative gearing for established homes bought after budget night, keeping it only for newly built properties, and also announced curbs to the capital gains tax discount on established dwellings. Negative gearing lets investors offset rental losses against other income. The government argued the housing market needed rebalancing, with most investor credit going towards existing homes rather than new supply. The major banks moved quickly to reflect the changes in how they assess investor loan applications, reducing borrowing capacity for many landlords. Those measures came on top of tighter lending rules. From February, the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority required banks to limit new loans at six or more times a borrower’s income to 20% of new mortgage lending, measured separately for owner-occupiers and investors. Monetary policy has added further pressure. The RBA has raised its cash rate five times this year, in February, March, May, September and November, taking it to 4.85%, the highest since 2008, as it fights inflation that has been pushed higher by energy costs. The November decision was split 6-3, and the statement dropped earlier language about further increases. The RBA’s own November Statement on Monetary Policy had already flagged a steep fall in investor lending, describing the drop in investor loan commitments as the largest in any hiking cycle on record. Governor Michele Bullock said a pullback in investor demand was normal in a housing downturn. The bigger fall compared with owner-occupiers, though, suggests the budget changes are having an effect. The figures strengthen the case that housing is cooling quickly, which may feed into the RBA’s assessment of whether its tightening has gone far enough. body: The broad-based jump in confidence, especially among service firms, adds to the picture of a Japanese economy strong enough to cope with higher interest rates. Combined with the reported tight labour market and persistent cost pressure, that could support expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening, which would be supportive for the yen. For equities, the strength in electronics and precision machinery reinforces the chip-led earnings story behind Japan’s tech and equipment names. The caution on passing costs on to customers is a reminder that margin pressure has not gone away. Japan Inc’s mood is at multi-year highs on chips and services, even as rising prices and borrowing costs start to pinch. Japanese manufacturers’ confidence climbed to its highest level in more than five years in November, lifted by booming semiconductor demand, while sentiment among non-manufacturers reached its strongest in over eight years, according to the Reuters Tankan poll. The manufacturers’ index rose to +27 from +22 in October, its highest reading since August 2021. The non-manufacturers’ index surged to +35 from +23, a level last seen in June 2018. The monthly poll is closely watched as a leading indicator for the Bank of Japan’s quarterly Tankan business survey. It was conducted from October 27 to November 6, and 214 of the 508 firms surveyed responded. Readings are calculated by subtracting the percentage of pessimistic responses from optimistic ones, so a positive figure signals net optimism. Chipmakers and their suppliers drove the gain among manufacturers. Sentiment in electronics jumped to +39 from +25, with one respondent describing demand for semiconductors, particularly memory chips, as very strong. Precision machinery, which includes some chip equipment makers, improved to +42 from +38 on robust domestic and overseas orders. Another machinery firm said shipments to the semiconductor market had reached unprecedented levels. Oil refining and ceramics rose to +25 from +14, while chemicals improved to +33 from +27. The service side of the economy was just as upbeat. Information and communications sentiment rose to +29 from +8 on strong orders, while services and others more than doubled to +43 from +19. One manager pointed to persistently tight labour market conditions keeping demand for staff high. Not everything was positive. Firms in both sectors said rising prices and higher interest rates were weighing on business, and some reported difficulty passing increased costs on to customers. Looking ahead, manufacturers expect sentiment to edge up to +28 in February, while non-manufacturers see confidence easing to +29, still well above recent levels. For the Bank of Japan, the combination of strong business confidence, a tight labour market and cost pressures will be one input as it weighs the outlook for policy. Its own quarterly Tankan will be the next major read on corporate sentiment. There's always something new to learn about the markets. Before the release, Fed Governor Christopher Waller had flagged a 0.3% reading as the point where a larger December hike could come into play. That’s what the report showed at published precision, and traders raised the odds of a half-point move. images.investinglive.com . The current numbers put a 50 bp hike in December at 10% while a 25 bp hike is the other 90%. Anthropic’s IPO terms gave tech stocks an early lift, but the Nasdaq Composite ended the session snapshot down 0.74%. investinglive.com The dollar gained the most against the Australian dollar, with AUDUSD down 0.91% to 0.6863, followed by a 0.75% decline in GBPUSD to 1.3339. EURUSD fell 0.55% to 1.1161, while USDJPY rose 0.55% to 158.77 (see technical post here) . The dollar’s smallest gain was against the Canadian dollar, with USDCAD up 0.51% to 1.4189. Core CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, the third straight month at 0.3% on a rounded basis. The BLS had no October 2025 comparison because of last year’s government shutdown, so the October report came without year-over-year readings. September’s annual rates were 3.7% for headline and 2.6% for core. Energy rose 0.7% after September’s 5.2% jump, helping explain the slowdown in headline CPI. Shelter rose 0.3% and accounted for more than 30% of the headline increase. Food rose 0.5%. Under the surface, motor vehicle insurance rose 0.7% and airfares climbed 0.4%, while used-car prices fell 1.2%. InvestingLive put core services excluding shelter, often called supercore, at roughly 0.4% for the month. The distinction for the Fed is that the energy impulse cooled sharply while core inflation held its pace. The unrounded core reading was 0.297%, close enough to Waller’s 0.3% marker to get the market’s attention. October PCE and November payrolls are still due before the December meeting. title: Middle East Oil Flows Far from Normal Despite Signs of Oversupply
summary: Crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the whole Middle Eastern region have recovered to close to pre-war levels, vessel-tracking services have been signaling for over a month now. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. On the face of it, an oversupply of crude oil could be forming. But the costs to refiners and consumers are not falling. War, insurance premiums, and record tanker rates have raised…
body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… Crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz and the whole Middle Eastern region have recovered to close to pre-war levels, vessel-tracking services have been signaling for over a month now. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. On the face of it, an oversupply of crude oil could be forming. But the costs to refiners and consumers are not falling. War, insurance premiums, and record tanker rates have raised the cost of transporting a barrel of crude oil from about $5 per barrel before the war to as much as $30 a barrel, and at times even higher. Middle Eastern producers are forced to slash their official selling prices to win customers because the surge in Persian Gulf exports is weakening the physical prices of local grades. Moreover, amid high freight costs, Middle East’s crude oil could only win Asia’s price-sensitive buyers with lower prices. The pricing of the Middle Eastern barrels and the weakening market structure of the benchmark Middle East crudes signal an oil glut is forming. But the shock to the global oil and fuel markets isn’t over as increased flows don’t mean traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has suddenly become less dangerous. In fact, attacks on vessels have intensified in the past month, while producers are tying up a large portion of the global tanker fleet on inefficient shuttle movements in and out of the Strait and subsequent ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Normal oil trade patterns from before the Iran war may never return. Until the market adapts to the new normal and Gulf producers build alternative supply routes, the war and insurance premium risks will remain with crude flows. Related: China’s Coal Buyers Resist Waiver Demands in New Indonesian Deals Hopes are high again in the past few days that the U.S. and Iran could reach an agreement, amid signals that President Donald Trump could pursue diplomacy instead of escalation following the crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm elections. In the past five trading days after the elections, Brent Crude prices slumped by about 17% to trade just above $91 per barrel early on Tuesday. The market has been blindsided by sudden breakdowns of attempts at talks on several occasions in the past eight months. The relative calmness after the elections in the U.S. and Israel, which weren’t positive for either Trump or Benjamin Netanyahu, may be only transitory. Regardless, the perceived near-term glut is pressuring the Middle East’s crude oil prices. The curve of the Dubai benchmark signaled last week that rising oil flows from the Middle East are exceeding demand for the first time since early July, when the three-week U.S.-Iran ceasefire allowed millions of barrels to leave unhindered the Strait of Hormuz. The November contract of the Dubai grade was in contango early last week, suggesting that concerns about the immediate lack of crude supply have eased significantly. Rising supply from the Middle East has also weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region are recovering and reaching pre-war levels on some days. Saudi oil giant Aramco last week slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount to the Middle East’s benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic. body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. South Sudan is courting fresh capital for 14 exploration blocks and a production increase from roughly 170,000 barrels per day to 230,000, which investors would find impossible to control once those barrels left the country. Captive to neighboring Sudan’s civil war, South Sudan is essentially divvying up its oil, under duress, between the Sudanese Army and the rival paramilitary RSF, which extract payment before the oil can reach the Red Sea. The government-backed South Sudan Oil & Power conference will put that proposition before investors in Juba at the end of the month, and its organizers place current production at 170,000 barrels per day, describing 230,000 bpd as a short-term target. A petroleum ministry official reported production of 175,000 bpd in August and set a lower target of 200,000 bpd by August 2027. Tanker tracking recorded eight cargoes carrying 4.8 million barrels from Sudan’s two Red Sea terminals in October, equivalent to combined Sudanese and South Sudanese exports of 155,000 bpd . Sudan’s Heglig fields were producing about 26,000 bpd in September, all of it sent for export, according to Sudan Tribune . Public data provide no current country breakdown and no reconciliation between South Sudan’s reported wellhead production and the volumes loaded at the Red Sea terminals. Juba’s lofty ambitions in the middle of the civil war in Sudan, which has effectively hijacked its exports, are an attempt to ride the tailwinds of the launch of the Africa Energy Bank. Afreximbank and the African Petroleum Producers’ Organisation formally established the institution in Abuja on October 31 with $5 billion in authorized capital . APPO Secretary-General Farid Ghezali said the bank had raised $500 million for deployment and would begin making investment decisions. Fresh capital can finance production inside South Sudan, but it can’t secure passage through Sudan. Crude from Blocks 1, 2 and 4 enters the Greater Nile pipeline through Heglig in West Kordofan, where Sudan’s paramilitary RSF displaced the Sudanese Army in December 2025. A tripartite agreement placed security inside the complex with the South Sudan People’s Defence Forces. South Sudanese troops now protect the installation, while the RSF dominates the surrounding territory and the Sudanese Army controls the Red Sea terminals at the other end of the line. Related: China’s Coal Buyers Resist Waiver Demands in New Indonesian Deals That division determines who is paid, how much, and by what means. A September report citing unnamed oil-industry sources says Juba gives the RSF $4 of the $11 charged on each South Sudanese barrel crossing territory under its control. The army-aligned government receives the remaining $7. South Sudan has previously settled pipeline obligations with crude , although no published account identifies whether the RSF’s current share is delivered in oil, cash or export proceeds. The Army’s portion provides more than compensation for operating a pipeline. Janes assesses that Sudanese processing and transit fees provide revenue used to sustain Army operations. The RSF collects its share in exchange for allowing the crude to cross territory it controls. Investors financing production connected to Heglig would add barrels to a trade that pays both forces. South Sudan’s second export line avoids Heglig, but doesn’t escape the war. The Petrodar pipeline carries Dar Blend from Blocks 3 and 7 at Paloch through six pumping stations in Sudan to the Bashair terminal on the Red Sea. A rupture in February 2024 cut South Sudan’s exports by roughly two-thirds and reduced production from about 150,000 bpd to 62,000 bpd. title: A ‘Geologic Freak’ in Arkansas Is Big Oil’s New Lithium Bet

body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… The world is electrifying at an unprecedented pace, and it’s only going to keep speeding up. COP 31, the latest iteration of the United Nations’ annual climate conference, kicked off today in Antalya, Türkiye, and achieving 35 percent global electrification by 2035 is going to be one of the event’s most central agenda items. Until extremely recently, this target likely would have seemed overly ambitious, but experts say that a number of factors, including volatile oil and gas markets stemming from the war in Iran, paired with enormous advances in clean energy technologies, have now put that goal within “striking distance.” All of that electrification is going to require a whole lot of lithium. Over the course of this decade alone, lithium demand has already skyrocketed by more than 400 percent on a global scale to top 1.5 million metric tons per year. Projecting out to 2035, the year featured in COP 31’s proposed electrification pledge, global demand could reach approximately 4 million tons. In the International Energy Agency’s Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 , no mineral is expected to see bigger demand growth. This is leading to increased competition over global lithium supply chains as nations rush to shore up their own future supplies to ensure long-term energy security in a rapidly changing energy landscape. But even as a diverse array of countries try to establish homegrown lithium production and refining sectors, one nation is expected to maintain an extreme degree of control over global supplies: China. Beijing controls an estimated 72 percent of the global lithium-ion market, and Chinese companies control a quarter of the world’s lithium mining capacity . This control runs up the supply chain as well: in 2024, more than 80 percent of battery cells on the planet were made in China, raising major concerns about geopolitical precarity and market resilience in clean energy supply chains. By 2030, Beijing is expected to control 39 percent of the world’s lithium production, according to a recent report from Wood Mackenzie. “Lithium production and lithium ownership are increasingly diverging, and it is reshaping the global critical mineral supply chains,” said Allan Pedersen, research director, energy transition & battery materials – lithium at Wood Mackenzie. “While production growth is becoming more geographically diverse, ownership remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies, mostly led by China.” By comparison, the United States produces just barely over 1 percent of the world’s lithium supplies, a large share of which comes from a single mine: Albemarle’s Silver Peak mine in Nevada. But that could all change thanks to an enormous, virtually untapped lithium reserve in southern Arkansas and East Texas known as the Smackover Formation . “It’s a geologic freak with its very high lithium concentrations,” Standard Lithium CEO David Park told Fortune . “We believe that our lands alone have the potential for over 150,000 tons per year of production.” Standard Lithium is expected to authorize its South West Arkansas Project (SWA) late this year, breaking ground on its initial 22,500-ton phase in the first quarter of next year. In late August, battery giant LG Energy Solution Ltd. signed a decade-long deal to buy 8,000 tons of battery-grade lithium carbonate annually from Smackover Lithium starting in 2029. Standard’s primary competitor, Texas-based EnergyX (short for Energy Exploration Technologies), already opened up a 250-ton pilot plant earlier this year, and aims to begin construction on its 15,000-ton Project Lonestar commercial facility by the end of 2027. body: API Shows Sharp Build in US Crude Oil, Distillate Inventories Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… The American Petroleum Institute (API) estimated that crude oil inventories in the United States rose by 9.0 million barrels in the week ending November 6. In the week prior, US crude oil inventories fell by 5.267 million barrels. Commercial crude oil inventories excluding the SPR have lost more than 54 million barrels over the last 30 weeks, and 3 million over this year, according to API data, which has been kept in check in part thanks to draws from the SPR. For the week ending November 6, 2.7 million barrels of crude oil left the SPR to aid commercial inventories, bringing the total inventory held in the SPR down to 279.5 million barrels —a level that is 434 million barrels shy of maximum capacity. The generally accepted operational minimum for oil in the SPR is between 250-300 million barrels, below which the reserve may find it difficult to pump and process oil efficiently. US production for the week ending Oct 30 reached a new record, rising to 14.003 million bpd in the period, up from 13.992 million bpd in the week prior, and up 352,000 bpd from a year ago. At 4:24 pm ET on Wednesday, Brent crude was trading down on the day at $91.96 (-0.66%). Brent is trading down more than $12 per barrel from this time last week. WTI was also trading down on the day, by $0.48 per barrel (-0.55%) at $86.37 , which is down roughly $11 per barrel since this time last week. Gasoline inventories rose by just 4 thousands barrels during the week ending November 6 (editor corrected) . In the week prior, gasoline inventories rose by 1.427 million barrels. In the week prior, gasoline inventories were 2% below the five-year average for this time of year, according to the latest EIA data. Distillate inventories also saw a build of 1.5 million barrels, compared to the 270,000 barrels lost in the week prior. Distillate inventories were 13% below the five-year average heading into this reporting period, the latest EIA data shows. Cushing inventory—the inventory kept at the delivery hub for the WTI Crude futures contract—gained 182,000 barrels after gaining 511,000 barrels in the previous week. title: American Barrick files for proposed IPO
summary: Barrick Mining announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation.
body: Barrick Mining (NYSE:B)(TSX:ABX) announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company, which will hold Barrick’s North American gold assets, will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation. The world’s third-biggest gold miner said it is moving forward with the proposed initial public offering (IPO) and has filed a registration statement on Form S-11 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in connection with the proposed IPO. American Barrick intends to apply to list its common stock on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker symbol ‘ABGC’. The number of shares to be offered and the proposed price range for the IPO have not yet been determined, the company said, adding that net proceeds from the IPO will be distributed to Barrick, which it expects to return to its shareholders. In September, chief executive officer Mark Hill said the planned North American gold IPO could slip into January. Hill, who was named in August to lead the North American unit after it goes public, said there had been “some delays” in working through formalities ahead of the listing. Barrick first announced last year its proposal to hive off its US assets from its sprawling portfolio in riskier countries. The new company will house Barrick’s joint-venture interests and the Fourmile discovery in the state of Nevada, which it has touted as “one of the century’s greatest gold discoveries.” Barrick struck a deal with Newmont in August that gave the Denver-based company a stake in Fourmile and brought the deposit into the joint Nevada Gold Mines venture in exchange for support of the planned IPO. Barrick Mining announced Tuesday that its planned new publicly listed company will be named American Barrick Gold Corporation.

title: Bitcoin price falls below $74,000 as hot US CPI fuels Fed rate hike fears - Crypto News
body: Bitcoin price has fallen below $74,000 after US inflation came in hotter than expected in October, raising concerns that the Federal Reserve could increase interest rates at its December meeting. According to crypto.news data, Bitcoin was trading around $73,784 on November 10, down approximately 1% over the past 24 hours after reaching an intraday high near $75,500. The cryptocurrency has lost 4.5% over the past week and more than 11% over the last 30 days, with the latest decline following the release of US consumer inflation figures that exceeded economists’ forecasts. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Tuesday that the Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% month over month in October, compared with economists’ expectations of 0.3%. Although headline inflation slowed from September’s 0.6% reading, the latest figure suggested that price pressures remained stronger than the Federal Reserve would have preferred. Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, exceeding the 0.2% increase economists had forecast. The report showed that shelter costs rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Food prices climbed 0.5%, while energy costs rose 0.7%, considerably slower than September’s 5.2% increase. The Labor Department did not publish annual inflation figures for October because last year’s government shutdown prevented officials from collecting the data needed for a year-over-year comparison. Following the release, Bitcoin briefly fell towards $73,500, while approximately $200 million in leveraged cryptocurrency positions were reportedly liquidated within five minutes. The selling followed an already difficult start to November, with investors increasingly concerned that persistent inflation could leave the Federal Reserve with little room to ease monetary policy. The latest inflation figures have strengthened expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December 9 meeting. According to Reuters, financial markets had fully priced in a 25 basis point increase, which would take the federal funds target range from 3.75%-4.00% to 4.00%-4.25%. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller had warned earlier Tuesday that policymakers should consider a larger 50 basis point increase if inflation remained stubbornly high. His comments came after stronger US employment figures showed that the economy added 165,000 jobs in October, giving policymakers another reason to maintain a restrictive monetary stance. Higher interest rates generally make interest-bearing assets more attractive and can reduce investors’ willingness to hold cryptocurrencies and other riskier investments. Bitcoin had already been struggling with uncertainty over interest rates before Tuesday’s report, particularly as expectations for another December increase continued to build. Investors will next receive the October Producer Price Index on November 13, followed by the Federal Reserve’s October meeting minutes on November 18. Beyond the inflation report, Bitcoin has faced sustained selling pressure from US spot exchange-traded funds. As crypto.news previously reported , spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $1.28 billion in net withdrawals between November 2 and November 6. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust accounted for roughly $1.21 billion of those withdrawals, while Fidelity’s FBTC attracted $93.1 million during the same period. The outflows continued on November 9, when investors withdrew another $201 million from US spot Bitcoin funds, including $213.2 million from BlackRock’s IBIT. Meanwhile, Bitfinex analysts found that Bitcoin’s earlier recovery towards $80,000 had been supported largely by leveraged futures positions, with direct spot buying remaining relatively weak. The cryptocurrency’s failure to reclaim $75,000 had already raised concerns about whether buyers could sustain another recovery without stronger institutional demand. Bitcoi

title: US raises 2026 Brent oil price forecast to $97.44 per barrel - Trend News Agency
body: BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 11. The U.S. Department of Energy has raised its forecast for the average price of Brent crude oil in 2026 by 1.2%, from $96.32 to $97.44 per barrel. This is according to a report by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), which operates under the Department of Energy. According to the report, oil prices increased for the third consecutive month in October. The rise was driven by declining global inventories, attacks on oil tankers in the Persian Gulf, limited maritime shipping capacity, and higher transportation costs. Combined, these factors contributed to a reduction in global oil supplies. The department expects Brent spot prices to remain at around $100 per barrel through the end of the year if current market conditions persist. According to the EIA's forecast, the average price of Brent crude oil will reach $85.78 per barrel in 2027.

title: Trump Signals End to War; Brent Crude Falls Below $90 to More Than Two-Month Low - finance.biggo.com
body: U.S. President Donald Trump has signaled that the U.S.-Iran conflict may be winding down, and with U.S. officials playing down the need to expand military operations, market concerns about a disruption to Middle East crude supplies have clearly eased. International oil prices fell for a second straight trading day, closing on November 10 at their lowest levels since late August. During the November 10 trading session, the front-month Brent Crude futures contract on ICE Futures Europe briefly broke below the $90-a-barrel mark, touching a low of $89.16 (about NT$2,900), before settling down 1.17% at $91.49 a barrel (about NT$3,000). December West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) fell 0.93% to settle at $86.04 a barrel (about NT$2,800). The selloff had already begun on November 9. Brent Crude's settlement price that day plunged $5.75, or 5.85%, to $92.57 a barrel (about NT$3,000), and selling pressure continued after the settlement, with post-settlement losses at one point widening to more than $7 a barrel (about NT$230). WTI's settlement price fell in tandem by $3.98, or 4.38%, to $86.85 a barrel (about NT$2,900), before dropping more than another $5 (about NT$160) in post-settlement trading. Trump said on November 8 that as long as negotiations continue to make progress, it is highly unlikely he would order a new round of attacks on Iran, describing the war as "essentially over." "At this point, it doesn't seem very necessary to take military action, but we are locked and loaded, ready for anything," he told reporters. The remarks eased concerns that the United States would expand strikes on Tehran after the midterm elections and served as the direct trigger for the sharp drop in oil prices. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said on November 10 that existing economic sanctions and the maritime blockade have been effective and that Washington sees no need for now to launch large-scale military operations against Iran. However, Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, denied the same day that Tehran was negotiating with Washington, prompting oil prices to rebound from their intraday lows and showing that the market remains wary of the Middle East situation. Supply-side tensions have not been fully eliminated. Both Iran and the United States said vessels were attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz, indicating that actual fighting has not truly ceased. A senior Iranian security official told state media that Tehran has no plans to negotiate unless Washington takes concrete action to fulfill the seven conditions listed in the temporary agreement reached in June. Trump was due to meet on November 10 with the prime minister of Qatar, which is playing a mediating role, but senior U.S. and Gulf officials remain skeptical about whether a deal can be reached quickly. ING analysts noted that as crude transportation through the Persian Gulf gradually recovers and the market anticipates a de-escalation of the U.S.-Iran conflict, the geopolitical risk premium in current oil prices continues to fade, but progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations and risks to energy facilities remain important variables. The demand side is also weighing on oil prices. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that global oil consumption will fall to 102.4 million barrels per day in 2026 from 104.4 million barrels per day in 2025. Persistent U.S. inflation pressure and rising expectations of interest rate hikes are also casting a shadow over the oil market's demand outlook. Oil prices hitting successive lows over two trading days reflects the market's rapid reassessment of Middle East geopolitical risk. For investors, short-term oil price moves will hinge closely on whether U.S.-Iran negotiations produce a substantive breakthrough and whether shipping safety in the Strait of Hormuz can genuinely improve. It expects inventories to rise in 2027 as net imports increase. US commercial crude oil inventories fell to their lowest October level since 2014, as exports rose and imports fell. title: US inflation tops forecasts, fueling December Fed rate hike bets | Daily Sabah - Daily Sabah
body: U.S. consumer prices rose faster than expected in October as higher food and housing costs fueled inflationary pressures, strengthening expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at its December policy meeting. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for a third straight month. It followed data last week showing the labor market regained ⁠momentum in October. Inflation is being driven by the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has ⁠boosted oil prices, the Trump administration's import tariffs, resilient consumer spending and aggressive business investment in artificial intelligence technology. The rising cost of living contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the midterm elections last week. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that "a stronger policy ​move may be needed." Waller also raised the prospect of an aggressive 50-basis-point hike. "The Fed seems to be falling behind the curve ​on ⁠inflation, and the October hold is looking like a policy mistake," said Stephen Juneau, an economist at Bank of America Securities. "We see a rising risk that the Fed will have to hike again in January, rather than March." The CPI increased 0.4% last month after advancing 0.6% in September, the department's Bureau of Labor Statistics said. It was the third consecutive month of gains of 0.4% or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI would climb 0.3% over the month. The BLS did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year's federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Some economists used the average index for September and November 2025 to estimate the year-over-year rate of change for the October CPI. Others used interpolated levels from independent sources. Their estimates for the October year-over-year CPI ranged from a gain of 3.9% to 4.0%. Annual consumer inflation was 3.7% in September. Shelter, which includes rents and hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly increase in the CPI. Shelter costs rose 0.3% after climbing 0.4% in September. Food prices surged 0.5% after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices climbed 0.4%, boosted by a 0.9% jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6%, while fruits and vegetables were 0.6% more expensive. Prices for dairy products increased 0.6%. The cost of snacks surged ⁠1.0%. Rising prices ⁠at the supermarket could be an early sign that high diesel prices are filtering through to consumers. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home rising 0.5% after a 0.2% gain in September. The cost of full-service meals jumped 0.7%. "This may finally be the beginning of a pass-through of higher transportation costs to grocery prices," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "If this is indeed happening, it could be a feature across a broad array of goods categories." Gasoline prices climbed 1.0% after soaring 9.1% in September. Consumers also paid more for electricity. Although diesel prices have eased off all-time highs, they remain on an upward trend, rising 2.7% in October after increasing 11.9% in September. Consumers could get some relief at the pump, with oil prices down at least 10% so far this month, but the pressure is unlikely to ease elsewhere, economists warned. Inflation-adjusted average weekly earnings fell again in October. The so-called core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy items, increased 0.3% in October for the third straight month. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed ⁠0.2% in October. Economists estimated that year-over-year core CPI inflation gained 2.8% in October. Jim Cramer Warns About the AI Data Center Trade. What It Means for Nvidia and Broadcom - 24/7 Wall St.
body: This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Jim Cramer is staying out of the AI infrastructure trade for now. On CNBC on November 10, 2026, he said: “I don’t want to make this trade because I still feel that you don’t want to be that linked to the data center yet.” He said it as the two biggest chip names in the expansion moved in opposite directions. NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) fell 5.22% to $169.35 in Tuesday morning trading. Broadcom ( NASDAQ:AVGO ) rose 3.21% to $329.72. Being “linked to the data center” means a stock’s earnings rise or fall with how much a small group of cloud providers and AI labs spend on servers. NVIDIA is about as linked as a company can be. In the quarter it reported in August, Data Center brought in $89.02 billion of $96.22 billion in total revenue, or about 93%. Its supply obligations reached $279 billion, mostly memory bought for Vera Rubin. Days sales outstanding increased to 60 days from 45. Those are large commitments to make before you know whether demand will hold. Broadcom has more margin, and that margin is shrinking. AI semiconductors made up 56% of total revenue in fiscal Q3, up from 49% in Q2, according to the company’s 8-K earnings release . Broadcom has six XPU customers and set up financing vehicles for two of them, Anthropic and OpenAI. Hock Tan said most AI computing demand “originates from this concentrated group who develop state-of-the-art frontier models.” He also raised a deployment risk: “Even as we ship the chips, will they be deployed on a timely basis?” NVIDIA is down 26.14% over the past month and 8.98% year to date. Part of that drop has nothing to do with data center demand. NVIDIA opened an investigation into its chief executive’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy , and the stock fell for a second day as investors considered what it could mean (The New York Times, CNBC). Other chip stocks rallied during the same stretch (CNBC). Broadcom is down 8.8% over the month and 4.21% for 2026. The other side of Cramer’s argument rests on valuation. NVIDIA trades at a trailing P/E of 36. Against consensus EPS of $15.9146 for the fiscal year ending January 2028, the multiple falls to about 11x. That EPS estimate has grown from $12.8148 90 days ago. Broadcom trades at roughly 17x fiscal 2027 consensus EPS of $19.4651. Management expects AI revenue of about $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and $230 billion in fiscal 2028, and says it has already secured supply for both years. Jensen Huang sees the same thing: “AI has reached its inflection point. It’s doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue.” Those low multiples only hold if the estimates turn out right, and the estimates vary widely. NVIDIA’s fiscal 2028 revenue estimates run from $506.48 billion to $778.47 billion. Broadcom’s fiscal 2027 estimates run from $114.72 billion to $200.12 billion. That wide spread shows how unsure analysts are about where AI spending is headed, which is Cramer’s point. For holders, the main question is concentration. NVIDIA gets most of its revenue from data centers. Broadcom has its VMware software business, which grew 29% last quarter, but AI chips make up a larger share of sales every quarter.
